title: Closer (2004) and Mike Nichols' Work: An Anti-RomCom

commenti.body:
>That's it, folks! Sorry for the lengthy text. What do you think about "Closer" and Nichols' career as a whole? I find him a fascinating director!

I brought up Nichols in an older thread on New Hollywood filmmakers that have, for whatever reason, never became names a la Scorsese or Coppola or Spielberg. Nichols, despite directing one of the classic, iconic New Hollywood films, is never really brought up as one of the greats. You certainly don't see him high on any of those "greatest directors of all time lists" or discussed as an auteur, as an artist.

I can think of two main reasons for this.

\`1. Film directing was only part of Nichols' career. He was also a very successful comedian and stage director; filmmaking was only one creative challenge he undertook.

2. Even a half-century after the pioneering *Cahiers du Cinéma* articles, auteurism is still an important influence on film criticism and discourse, and Nichols, as a director who never wrote his own screenplays, can be seen as lacking auteur cred. This is probably compounded by the fact that many of the screenwriters he collaborated with were renowned writers who had their own auteur status: Buck Henry, Aaron Sorkin, Nora Ephron, Elaine May, Neil Simon, etc. In other words, situations where the actual "authorship" (if you're the kind of person who thinks that there must be a single author) is in question and where a certain kind of auteurist critic could dismiss Nichols as just a director, rather than an all-around auteur.

Auteur theory is first used in Francois Truffaut's book of Hitchcock, who didn't write his movies. Scorsese, Spielberg, Lumet, Altman generally don't/didn't write their movies, and they are generally considered auteurs. Yasujiro Ozu, Kenji Mizoguchi, Frank Capra, et al.


I see what you're getting at, but their are many examples of directors considered to be auteurs who didn't have the same creative control that the most auteuristic of directors (like Tarantino, Cassavetes, or Wong Kar Wai).


I think the issue with Nichols is he doesn't seem to have any unifying themes, idiosyncracies, or just a general style where you say, "Oh yeah, that's Mike Nichols!!!"


Mind you, I'm not arguing about the quality of any director's works here, Nichols just never seemed to have anything to me that really stands out as being "Nicholian" in the same way you would see a scene blocked by Spielberg and know immediately who the director is.

To be fair, Scorsese wrote or cowrote seven of his feature films, earning two Best Adapted Screenplay nominations. Altman cowrote *McCabe & Mrs. Miller*, *Images*, *Buffalo Bill and the Indians*, *Short Cuts*, etc. and is credited as the sole screenwriter on *3 Women*. Yasujiro Ozu cowrote all of his postwar films with Kogo Noda. Spielberg wrote *Close Encounters of the Third Kin*d by himself, and cowrote *A.I.*, *Poltergeist*, and *The Fabelmans*. In other words, all of these filmmakers have had significant success as screenwriters and that at least contributes something to their auteur status. And, re: Hitchcock, everything I've read about him (including books and interviews by writers like Evan Hunter/Ed McBain and Ernest Lehman) really makes me think that he was really the uncredited cowriter of his classic films.

The key current filmmakers who arguably have auteur status while being "just directors" would be Ridley Scott and David Fincher.

While Truffaut's book on Hitchcock may have popularized the concept of auteur theory, he had been writing about the concept in journal articles since 1954 and the term had already become known in English-language film criticism (via Andrew Sarris) by the time that book came out in 1966.

>I think the issue with Nichols is he doesn't seem to have any unifying themes, idiosyncracies, or just a general style where you say, "Oh yeah, that's Mike Nichols!!!"

This is a good point and probably the third key reason for his lack of auteur status. Although OP seems to see some consistent themes in his films across the decades. Thinking about his filmography as a whole, are there any common motifs or narrative elements that stand out to you?

Yeah, I was being a little reductive on saying these directors didn't write their films. Whether credited or not, you do see flourishes that seem very consistent throughout their career. Even films Spielberg didn't write, like Saving Private Ryan or Jurassic Park, there are moments that feel like he had a deep hand in how that scene was written, if he didn't write it himself.


What I should have said, is these directors aren't themselves known as being adroit screenwriters, such as Tarantino, even though they do commit to ensuring that every script is guided by them either directly by writing or intense editing.




The moment I hit send on the previous post, I wanted to revise what I said about Nichols not having a general theme he gravitated towards. OP nailed it by linking the general nihilism in examining relationships throughout his films. There's a belief that many of his characters have that maybe romance will be the answer to a corporatized sense of disillusion with the modern world--but these relationships end in failure, either by situation or by having incorrectly diagnosed the underlying issue with your feelings about the world. Hell, even Wolf, as bad a movie as it is, deals with this malaise.


Maybe that's the other thing, too, he has a good amount of stinkers that probably held his legacy back. Not that Scorsese also didn't have stinkers, but he appears to have been less impacted by them.


(I'm just bragging right now, but I appreciate you recognizing the distinction between Evan Hunter/Ed McBain. He was my great uncle. Though, the family had a falling out with him after he changed his name to Evan Hunter... Kurosawa's High and Low is based on one of his novels, FYI).

Yes, Hunter/McBain is the one step between Kurosawa and Hitchcock if you're playing six degrees of Kevin Bacon. Have you read his book on Hitchcock? It's basically a memoir of his work on *Alfred Hitchcock Presents* and *The Birds*.

The theme of nihilism (and a desperate need to find meaning in romance) is also very present in *Carnal Knowledge*, maybe his most overlooked and underrated film.

Love Nichols. I randomly came across Closer on netflix last year, never heard of it, saw it had a killer cast, and gave it a try. I loved it, it's a modern masterpiece imo. I need to watch more of his films, I just watched Carnal Knowledge the other day which was also INCREDIBLE, I would highly recommend that if you liked closer. Very similar themes, another great cast, pretty much a perfect film imo. And I still haven't even seen Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf! I'm sure I'll love it, maybe I'll watch it tonight lol.
Any thoughts on Nichols' legacy and why he's not really thought of as an auteur? I mentioned a few possibilities earlier in this thread.

That's an interesting question. I went to film school and we certainly discussed the auteur theory, but it was talked about more as something that someone either believed in or didn't, i.e. either every director is an 'auteur' or none of them are.

Given the heirarchical structure in which all films are made, above the line, below the line etc, I don't see how someone like Nichols could not be considered an auteur under that theory. A great script still needs great directon to make it a great movie. Can a terrific script survive sub-par directing? I'm not sure. Can a half baked script be turned into something great with direction? I think it can.

And then you have the editing afterwards, which can either make or break a movie... there are so many steps along the chain, the whole 'auteur theory' thing seems a bit silly to me. No matter what someone's position is, I think if they're involved in multiple legendary productions, they're probably really good at what they do. I'm sure there have been fantastic directors who filmed something magic, and then it was butchered in the editing room, and then it reflected poorly on them. But I digress.

Even if you believed that someone could fluke direct a brilliant movie, Nichols has multiple of those, so you couldn't say he's a fluke. I think he deserves to be considered as legendary a director and 'auteur' as anybody.

>That's an interesting question. I went to film school and we certainly discussed the auteur theory, but it was talked about more as something that someone either believed in or didn't, i.e. either every director is an 'auteur' or none of them are.

This isn't directly related to Mike Nichols, but I'm not sure this all-or-nothing approach to auteurism really reflects reality. One obvious objection would be that there have clearly been at least a few auteur producers in Hollywood history: David O. Selznick, Walt Disney, Val Lewton, etc. Is *Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs* a Walt Disney film or a David Hand film? 

And the origins of auteur theory, in fifties French film criticism, explicitly pitted auteurs against directors for hire who merely supervised the translation of a screenplay. 

For what it's worth, I agree with you. Any feature film is necessarily a team effort.

I think one additional factor in Nichols' lack of legendary status is the perception (not saying that I necessarily agree with it) that, after a few groundbreaking New Hollywood films, he spent a lot of his creative energy on Broadway and became a filmmaker for hire who directed unchallenging mainstream movies. 

In the words of David Thomson,

>Mike Nichols is an unquestioned figure in our culture, a smart man, a funny man, a proven success in cabaret, on records, as a stage director, and as a deliverer of talking-point movies—movies that are smart, funny, “adult,” “on the pulse,” and “of their moment.” Yet I find it hard to grasp him in there, a movie director: after fifteen or so films, is there anything more substantial than a high reputation and a producer’s instinct for what smart people might want to see?

I really appreciate the shoutout! I don't think I was explicit about my skepticism about auteur theory in terms of the way it holds directors in the highest regard.


Val Lewton is a great example. You can sort of tell when a film is his based on production. What I think is lost on director-focused auteur theory is that many of them are also producers and collaborators.


I went to film school with a fairly highly regarded producer in Hollywood. I asked him for advice, and if he'd assist me with a project. He told me no, he only invests in a project where he can have creative control from beginning to end.


Producers have a massive impact on film, creatively. They can choose topics. Choose screenwriters, directors. Ultimately, this is why THEY get the award for best picture.


The most highly regarded directors also become producers, and that's when they make their best work. I don't know how much Nichols dabbled in the producer aspect. He might be more like a Sydney Pollack situation where he's elevating the work because of his excellent direction, but there's just something missing. Something hard to identify that stops him from becoming next level.

I'm embarrassed to say, I haven't read his book on his relationship with Hitchcock, Me and Hitch. Part of it is I don't love Hitchcock, and, I hate to say it, I've tried to read the 87th precinct series, but I'm so uninspired by it. So of its time. I kind of want to preserve my mythology of my family without getting disappointed.


For family reasons, I know should read it. King's Ransom inspired one of my favorite Kurosawa movies, and Blackboard Jungle is legitimately great.


I finally learned to appreciate The Birds, though. It looks me decades and repeat viewings.
